newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Shell spoils oil results party.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Shell spoils oil results party.

text.p: Royal Dutch/Shell Group on Thursday spoiled the party mood among oil industry investors as it presented a disappointing second-quarter performance.
The Anglo-Dutch oil giant turned in lower results after British Petroleum and the five U.S. majors had surprised markets with better than expected earnings.
Shell blamed its chemicals sector, while also pointing at the pound's strength and inventory losses as reasons for not meeting market forecasts.
The group's net earnings excluding special items fell four percent to 1.140 billion pounds ($1.8 billion) from 1.187 billion a year ago, while a profit rise had been expected.
Shell shares, which have had a strong run recently, were down four pence to 469 in London at 1255 GMT but had earlier hit as low as 440p.
In Amsterdam, shares in the Dutch arm, Royal Dutch Petroleum, fell 1.90 guilders to 118.40.

Analysts were revisiting their full-year forecasts for the company after the disappointing results. Brokerage house Credit Lyonnais Laing cut its full year estimates by 10 percent and SocGen analysts downgraded the company to "sell" from "hold".
"We had a strong second half last year which we don't envisage this year and we don't expect the underlying environment to improve," said analyst Jurjen Lunshof at Credit Lyonnais Laing.
Shell said its results were hit by currency losses of 117 million pounds. This was due to sterling's strength in the second quarter, which masked an underlying three percent profit rise.
Higher production offset lower crude oil prices, while chemical earnings were slightly down in the quarter, Shell said.
Chairman Mark Moody-Stuart said the chemicals' sector performance was "disappointing", but he was optimistic for the 1997 second half as a major restructuring programme continued.
"I am confident that by the end of the year we will be ahead of our original road map targets," he said.
Chemicals profits fell one percent in the second quarter due to one-off items such as plant start-up costs in Singapore, Moody-Stuart said.
Another negative "blip" was the fact Shell took 70 percent of its plant maintenance costs in the three months to June 30, he added.
Shell's refining and marketing margins were up 17 percent in the quarter on a current cost basis, but reported earnings were lower because of inventory holding losses.
Crude oil prices in the first half were about $1.50 a barrel below a year earlier due to resumption of exports from Iraq and increased non-OPEC production.
The oil price decline as well as lower gas sales resulted in a 10 percent decline in exploration and production profits.
Shell said the outlook was for continued increases in crude oil supply from the North Sea and ample supply of oil products.
The group spent 1.7 billion pounds on capital investment and exploration in the quarter and said spending was set to step up in the second half, mainly on exploration and production.
After BP on Tuesday announced share buy-back plans, cash-rich Shell would not rule out it might do the same once the Dutch tax regime had changed.

"At the moment in the Netherlands it is simply impractical for Royal Dutch," Moody-Stuart said. "But that I think may well change and then it may be something we could look at," he added. ($ = 0.624 British Pounds)
